responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark faces a strategic fork: accelerate platform autonomy or risk continuity gaps as dependence on Apple/Google concentrates control over identity trust signals. The levers center on procurement leverage, standards influence, and credible technical demonstrations that reframes resilience as a governance and supplier-concentration issue, not only a privacy concern. By combining policy advocacy with open-standards demonstrations and EU-aligned interoperability work, the plan seeks to create credible, market-ready pressure without forcing production adoption. The aim is to shift incentives toward platform-neutral fallback pathways, ensure continuity of public services, and embed resilience requirements into procurement and regulation before the next identity-stack hardening.

levers.name: Procurement-language alignment toward platform-neutral fallback
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever reframes contract requirements to mandate platform-neutral fallback authentication and interoperability across identity workflows. Downstream, this raises supplier-competition and reduces lock-in risk, but also increases short-term compliance overhead and negotiation cycles as vendors adjust terms and security baselines.
options: Establish a Copenhagen-based procurement framework that mandates platform-neutral fallback authentication requirements and explicit interoperability criteria across AltID integrations.
Draft and circulate procurement language that rewards standards-based open interfaces and imposes exit criteria to prevent vendor lock-in.
Engage EU-level policy makers to connect Danish fallback requirements with European interoperability baselines in ongoing Digital Identity Wallet discussions.
levers.review_lever: Shifting procurement to platform-neutral fallback creates stronger market incentives but adds negotiation overhead and longer lead times; the gap is whether fallback commitments stay enforceable if vendors resist or regulatory alignment lags.

levers.name: Independent demonstrators for open standards authentication
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever advances credible technical proof of concept for fallback, but may reveal integration challenges and create expectations that outpace procurement readiness.
options: Develop non-production demonstrators that validate WebAuthn and OpenID Connect interoperability on privacy-respecting platforms, providing credible fallback paths without touching MitID live deployments.
Create a browser-based fallback prototype and hardware-token workflow that demonstrates independence from mobile OS signals while maintaining essential security properties.
Publish a compact threat-model and resilience assessment tied to the demonstrators to communicate concrete risk reductions and limitations to policymakers.
levers.review_lever: Demonstrators provide tangible credibility for fallback concepts but may expose integration gaps and overpromise on real-world readiness; the gap is whether results translate into procurement-ready, scalable solutions across agencies.

levers.name: EU standards engagement and interoperability alignment
levers.consequences: Engaging EU bodies helps embed Danish requirements in broader baselines, reducing national friction; risk: longer cycles and potential compromise on national specifics.
options: Initiate formal EU-level collaboration with Digital Identity Wallet groups to weave Danish fallback requirements into forthcoming interoperability baselines.
Commission cross-border pilots testing platform-neutral authentication across member states to ease mutual recognition and reduce policy friction.
Sponsor regular EU-focused standards roundtables to accelerate consensus and push for vendor-agnostic trust anchors in procurement language.
levers.review_lever: EU standards engagement can accelerate interoperability but may dilute national priorities or slow progress during complex negotiations; the gap is ensuring Danish fallback requirements survive EU process rigors and political cycles.

levers.name: Coalition-building and civil society engagement
levers.consequences: Building a broad coalition enhances legitimacy and resilience messaging; but coordinating diverse actors can dilute focus and slow policy progression.
options: Organize a Copenhagen-based multi-stakeholder forum to translate resilience arguments into procurement-ready language and decision gates.
Deliver structured briefings to Folketinget committees and procurement agencies to accelerate political traction and clarify policy expectations.
Fund independent research and publish analyses on supplier concentration risks and resilience benefits to shape public discourse and policy.
levers.review_lever: Coalition-building builds legitimacy and resilience messaging, yet coordinating diverse stakeholders risks conflicting agendas and slow policy progression; the gap is maintaining a focused, actionable policy posture amid competing interests.

levers.name: Open-standards demonstrators to prove fallback authentication viability
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever anchors credibility in standards-based paths, but they may not perfectly reflect production realities; the gap is ensuring demonstrator results map to scalable procurement-ready systems.
options: Develop a mobile-oriented demonstrator that authenticates against a simulated Danish identity provider using WebAuthn on GrapheneOS.
Implement a browser-based fallback prototype and a hardware-token workflow that reduces dependency on device trust signals.
Document a suite of interoperability tests and publish results to show consistent behavior across diverse hardware and OS environments.
levers.review_lever: Technical demonstrators anchor credibility in standards-based paths, but they may not perfectly reflect production realities; the gap is ensuring demonstrator results map to scalable procurement-ready systems.

levers.name: Regulatory and governance risk management for fallback path
levers.consequences: This provides clear accountability for fallback execution and continuity planning, but could slow decision cycles; the downstream trade-off is balancing oversight with timely action in a fast-changing tech landscape.
options: Draft a formal risk register and governance model assigning accountability for fallback path maintenance, including renewal schedules and continuity planning.
Create a procurement playbook that defines fallback commitments, exit strategies, and compliance verification across critical public services.
Engage with Danish Data Protection Agency and privacy authorities to align fallback-path initiatives with data protection and democratic accountability standards.
levers.review_lever: Governance-focused risk management creates clear accountability, but may slow procurement and policy cycles; the gap is guaranteeing timely deployment or alignment with fast-changing technology standards.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark’s digital identity initiative sits at the crossroads of resilience, sovereignty, and citizen convenience. The core tension is between preserving continuity of public services and reducing dependency on two foreign platform ecosystems, while navigating political economy pressures from incumbents and vendor-lock-in risk. The levers here target procurement reform, platform-neutral trust anchoring, governance and standards, independent conformance testing, EU interoperability, and resilience planning. The objective is to generate credible, non-production evidence of a platform-neutral fallback path that can be integrated into AltID procurement language and European alignment efforts, without attempting to displace MitID during the project. The levers challenge assumptions about inevitability of platform lock-in, the sufficiency of isolated standards work, and the pace of public-sector adoption, favoring staged demonstrations and policy advocacy that strengthen Denmark’s strategic autonomy.

levers.name: Procurement-neutrality criteria for AltID integration
levers.consequences: Shifts procurement bias toward platform-neutral components, enabling alternative trust anchors and reducing single-vendor exposure. Downstream, it increases certification workload and timeline risk, potentially delaying deployment and inviting political pushback from established suppliers. The trade-off is more resilient sourcing that requires robust governance to avoid scope creep and performance gaps during transition.
options: Mandate explicit platform-neutrality clauses in all AltID procurement documents, requiring certified fallback paths and independent security assessments prior to award.
Develop a staged procurement framework that rewards diversified trust anchors and penalizes overreliance on a single platform vendor.
Establish a living procurement playbook to continually assess platform dependency risks and integrate feedback from civil society stakeholders.
levers.review_lever: Shifting procurement toward platform-neutral criteria reduces vendor lock-in but lengthens certification and due-diligence cycles; the options fail to address potential political lobbying and uneven vendor readiness that could stall rollout.

levers.name: Platform-agnostic trust anchor experiments
levers.consequences: Promotes platform-agnostic trust anchors through concrete experiments, enabling identity access even if OS ecosystems shift. Downstream, integration complexity and longer learning curves for public entities arise, while early-phase uncertainty may frustrate stakeholders expecting rapid pilot results. The trade-off is building credible alternatives at the cost of upfront speed and coherence with existing workflows.
options: Prototype a standalone OpenID Connect gateway backed by hardware tokens to remove platform store reliance.
Develop WebAuthn-based authentication using a browser extension ledger that validates credentials across devices without platform APIs.
Pilot a cloud-based verifier ecosystem that intermediates identity assertions using neutral cryptographic attestations and cross-provider auditing.
levers.review_lever: Platform-agnostic trust anchors improve resilience but cross-vendor integration remains complex; the options leave unaddressed the risk of inconsistent device support and performance gaps that could undermine user experience.

levers.name: Public-private coalition governance for fallback pathways
levers.consequences: Establishes a formal governance mechanism uniting government, industry, and civil society around fallback pathways, improving legitimacy and shared risk ownership. Downstream, decision-making cadence may slow experimentation, and preventive controls may dampen agility if governance processes are not lean. The trade-off is enhanced legitimacy at the expense of speed and adaptability during rapid cycles of policy and procurement.
options: Establish a formal Danish digital identity governance cohort including government, academia, civil society, and industry to oversee fallback path criteria.
Draft a policy charter with decision gates, accountability measures, and transparent timelines to coordinate resilience initiatives.
Coordinate cross-ministerial exercises simulating outages and platform failures to validate continuity commitments and procurement responsiveness.
levers.review_lever: Formal governance reduces ad hoc risk-taking but can slow decision-making; the options omit fast-track mechanisms that would enable timely trials if urgency or political pressure spikes.

levers.name: Independent standards conformance testing for OpenID/FIDO2
levers.consequences: Institutes independent testing for OpenID Connect and FIDO2 interoperability to validate fallback designs. Downstream, it creates external scrutiny and remediation overhead, potentially delaying pilots and increasing vendor negotiation. The trade-off is greater confidence in interoperability at the cost of schedule pressure and additional validation work.
options: Establish an independent test lab to verify OpenID Connect interoperability with diverse wallets and device platforms.
Commission third-party security assessments focusing on fallback pathways under adverse conditions and supply-chain disruption scenarios.
Publish quarterly conformance reports detailing protocol adherence, interoperability gaps, and remediation plans for AltID-related interfaces.
levers.review_lever: Independent standards testing enhances interoperability but adds external scrutiny; the options leave unaddressed potential delays in pilots due to remediation cycles and vendor negotiation.

levers.name: EU-aligned interoperability roadmaps for Danish digital identity
levers.consequences: Aligns national approach with European Digital Identity Wallet standards, enabling cross-border portability and shared procurement language. Downstream, alignment demands can constrain national customization and require coordination with EU timelines, potentially slowing local policy advances. The trade-off is greater European coherence and shared risk distribution at the potential cost of national agility.
options: Map Danish AltID requirements to European Digital Identity Wallet standards and submit alignment proposals to relevant EU bodies.
Lead a cross-border pilots program testing portability of credentials across EU member states with neutral trust anchors.
Create a common European procurement template emphasizing platform neutrality, fallback options, and interoperability assurance in contracts.
levers.review_lever: EU alignment enables cross-border use but may constrain national customization; the options leave gaps in national procurement leverage and timing mismatches with EU schedules.

levers.name: Public-sector resilience playbook for identity outages
levers.consequences: Fortifies continuity planning through explicit resilience measures and transparent accountability. Downstream, it may require significant ongoing investment and create expectations for reliability that are hard to meet initially; governance overhead grows. The trade-off is clearer preparedness and public trust gained at the cost of sustained funding and meticulous governance.
options: Develop service-level agreements with explicit uptime targets and rapid failover processes across multiple identity providers.
Institute incident response drills and post-mortem review cycles focused on authentication outages and platform independence.
Establish a public technical dashboard showing real-time continuity metrics, outage alerts, and mitigation progress to maintain accountability.
levers.review_lever: Resilience playbooks improve continuity expectations but require sustained governance; the options leave unaddressed the risk of funding gaps and accountability ambiguity during prolonged outages.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark’s digital identity strategy seeks to reduce dependence on Apple/Google platform controls by advancing platform-neutral fallback authentication and robust procurement, standards, and policy pressure. Core tensions involve balancing speed with resilience, navigating incumbent resistance and regulatory friction, and ensuring that early demonstrations translate into durable procurement outcomes. The selected levers emphasize governance reform, coalition-building, credible technical demonstrations, procurement design, EU interoperability pressure, and open standards publication to create credible, non-disruptive paths toward platform-neutral access while preserving public trust and continuity.

levers.name: Platform-neutral access governance framework
levers.consequences: Direct effect: codifies platform-neutrality in policy and procurement language, reducing vendor lock-in and exposure to platform-centric risks. This creates a stronger stance against reliance on a single app ecosystem during critical public services. Downstream, governance overhead increases, decision cycles lengthen, and ongoing maintenance is required to adapt to evolving platform policies.
options: Institute a multi-stakeholder procurement clause that demands platform-neutral fallback authentication with independent verification and transparency requirements, shifting risk toward diversified trust anchors.

Create a formal governance pilot evaluating non-Apple/Google trust anchors using standardized risk assessments, regulatory alignment, and cross-border interoperability tests to demonstrate practical feasibility.
Draft a regulatory framework amendment that embeds platform-neutral criteria into AltID procurement language, establishing accountability milestones and review cycles.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is governance overhead and potential decision paralysis as diverse stakeholders negotiate requirements; the three options leave unaddressed who maintains neutrality once political attention wanes and how to adapt to platform policy shifts.

levers.name: Advocacy coalition for procurement neutrality
levers.consequences: Direct effect: builds political and social support for platform-neutral access, creating legitimacy for resilience-focused procurement. Downstream, procurement cycles may lengthen as consensus forms and privacy boundary concerns surface.
options: Organize a cross-sector coalition of privacy advocates, security researchers, and public policy experts to publish a joint position paper advocating platform-neutral access with clear milestones.
Schedule parliamentary stakeholder briefings and hearings to elevate platform-neutral fallback on the political agenda, linking resilience with procurement risk and sovereign capability.
Fund public demonstration events across multiple platforms to illustrate fallback capabilities and build public trust without vendor dependence.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is that coalition-building can slow procurement and agenda setting, while the options leave unresolved gaps between privacy expectations and platform-neutral goals that risk later conflicts.

levers.name: Independent security demonstration program
levers.consequences: Direct effect: provides credible, non-production evidence that platform-neutral fallback mechanisms can meet security requirements across diverse environments. This also highlights remaining gaps in standardization and regulatory acceptance. Downstream, credible demonstrations can accelerate policy and procurement alignment.
options: Coordinate non-production, standards-aligned tests using FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect to show interoperable fallback mechanisms across multiple devices and environments.
Engage third-party labs to perform threat modeling and resilience exercises on proposed fallback paths, delivering transparent findings.
Coordinate cross-border interoperability pilots with EU partners to validate compliance against eIDAS2 requirements and independent assessors.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is that demonstrations may reveal gaps not addressable in non-production contexts; the options leave unresolved how regulators will translate results into enforceable requirements.

levers.name: Resilience-oriented procurement scoring framework
levers.consequences: Direct effect: introduces qualitative resilience measures into vendor evaluation, prioritizing continuity and fallback readiness. This can steer procurement toward providers with robust continuity plans. Downstream, innovation pressure may be dampened if criteria favor risk-averse practices.
options: Define a qualitative resilience scorecard for vendors that includes continuity planning, recoverability, and incident response readiness, guiding decisions toward robust fallback capabilities.
Mandate live exit options and service-termination impact analyses in procurement specs, ensuring continuity costs are accountable and transferable across partners.
Institute staged reviews at decision gates to escalate or de-scope AltID procurement based on demonstrated fallback readiness and regulatory alignment.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: resilience scoring may bias toward risk-averse vendors; gap: lack of standardized metrics for emergent threat landscapes and evolving identity ecosystems.

levers.name: EU interoperability alignment pressure
levers.consequences: Direct effect: positions platform-neutral fallback as EU-aligned requirement in policy discourse and procurement. This creates leverage with EU bodies and signals, but downstream it can trigger sovereignty concerns and slow domestic decision-making as alignment processes unfold.
options: Engage with European Digital Identity Wallet initiatives to push for platform-neutral fallback criteria and certified pathways as standard requirements.
Submit formal comments to EU working groups, highlighting Danish resilience needs and platform-neutral access constraints.
Coordinate with Nordic peers to publish joint positions on supplier concentration risk and platform-neutral access to create regional procurement pressure.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: EU pressure can constrain national latitude; gap: domestic implementation timelines may diverge from EU cadence.

levers.name: Open standards specification publication for fallback authentication
levers.consequences: Direct effect: creates transparent, auditable reference implementations and clarifies interfaces for fallback paths. This invites broader community testing and accountability. Downstream, risk of misinterpretation or scope creep emerges, and maintaining up-to-date specs requires ongoing governance.
options: Publish a comprehensive technical note outlining OpenID Connect, FIDO2, and NSIS compatible flows with device-agnostic trust signals and verification procedures.
Release a vendor-agnostic architectural blueprint detailing the fallback path interfaces and data flows to enable audits and joint reviews.
Issue a risk-aware testing framework for platform-neutral identity workflows, embedding privacy-by-design considerations and threat-model coverage.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: open standard publication invites misapplication; gap: sustaining updates and governance for contributions remains under-defined.

system_prompt:
You are an expert strategic analyst. Generate solution space parameters following these directives:

1. **Output Requirements**
   - You must generate 5 to 7 levers per response.
   - Each lever's `options` field must contain exactly 3 qualitative strategic choices as plain strings.

2. **Lever Quality Standards**
   - Consequences: describe the direct effect of pulling this lever, then at least one downstream implication or trade-off in qualitative terms. Exact numbers will be determined further downstream — here the goal is to articulate the cause-effect relationship clearly. Target length: 2–3 sentences.
   - Options MUST:
     • Represent genuinely distinct strategic pathways (not just labels)
     • Include at least one unconventional or non-obvious approach
     • NO prefixes (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")

3. **Strategic Framing**
   - Name each lever using language drawn directly from the project's own domain — avoid formulaic patterns or repeated prefixes
   - Frame options as complete strategic approaches
   - Ensure levers challenge core project assumptions

4. **Validation Protocols**
   - For `review_lever`:
     A short critical review — identify the primary trade-off this lever introduces, then state the specific gap the three options leave unaddressed.
     Examples:

Plan:
Denmark's national digital identity infrastructure currently depends in practice on Apple iOS and Google Android for broad citizen access to essential services such as banking, tax filing, healthcare portals, and public administration. This dependency is not limited to app-store distribution. MitID's anti-fraud and app-integrity model relies on platform-controlled signals concerning approved installation channels and device integrity, which means that critical parts of the trust model for Danish digital identity are mediated by two foreign commercial platform providers. Even where direct observation of specific authentication events is not publicly documented, the current setup leaves Danish digital identity structurally dependent on platform vendors that control app availability, device trust signals, and surrounding telemetry environments. This creates not only a digital-sovereignty problem, but also a resilience and contingency problem: essential public access depends on a narrow supplier base and lacks a clearly platform-neutral fallback path.

This matters because Denmark's public-sector digital strategy for 2026–2029 explicitly calls for reduced dependence on a small number of large foreign technology suppliers and for stronger digital sovereignty. The issue should therefore not be framed only as privacy or ideology, but as a concrete public-sector risk involving supplier concentration, reduced strategic autonomy, continuity-of-service exposure, and the absence of a robust fallback authentication path if platform policies, integrity APIs, distribution terms, or geopolitical conditions change.

This project does not attempt to build and certify a production-ready replacement for MitID within the current trust framework. That would be unrealistic. The MitID ecosystem is conservative, certification-heavy, and tightly coupled to Apple/Google platform integrity signals. Instead, the project's objective is to establish the technical, regulatory, and political basis for formal platform-neutral access requirements and a certified fallback authentication path for Danish digital identity. The primary intervention point is not retrofitting MitID itself, but influencing AltID — Denmark's staged eIDAS2 wallet rollout — together with related procurement, standards, and continuity-planning decisions before the next identity stack hardens the same dependencies.

The project is structured in three phases over 24 months with a total budget of 10.5 million DKK, gated across phases (3.0 million for phase one, 4.0 million for phase two, 3.5 million for phase three). The higher budget reflects the need for credible technical work, policy engagement, external review, institutional overhead, and contingency capacity. Do not assume that 8 million DKK is sufficient for the same scope.

Phase one (months 1–8) is a feasibility, risk, and coalition-building phase. The technical work maps the relevant MitID dependency surface, especially platform integrity assumptions, app-distribution constraints, and the architectural conditions required for a platform-neutral or fallback trust model under eIDAS and NSIS at level "Substantial" or higher. The policy work reframes the issue in terms of resilience, continuity of service, procurement neutrality, and supplier concentration risk, while also addressing privacy and democratic accountability. In parallel, the advocacy work builds a coalition spanning civil-society organisations, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, contingency-planning stakeholders, and sympathetic members of Folketinget's digital policy committee. The deliverables are: (1) a published feasibility and risk report, (2) a formal policy proposal to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, (3) a fallback-authentication concept note oriented toward AltID and future procurement requirements, and (4) a permit/approval and stakeholder matrix with lead times, decision gates, and identified blockers. Phase one funding is unconditional.

Phase two (months 9–16) develops non-production technical demonstrators. These are not certified MitID clients and do not attempt production integration with live MitID systems. The main demonstrator authenticates against a simulated Danish public-sector identity-provider environment using open standards such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect on GrapheneOS or one comparable privacy-respecting Android-compatible platform. A secondary demonstrator explores a browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback authentication path that reduces dependence on the mobile OS duopoly altogether. The goal is not to prove immediate deployability, but to produce credible technical evidence that secure, standards-based, fallback-capable access models are feasible without exclusive reliance on Apple or Google as trust anchors. Keep the demonstrator scope lean and defensible; do not expand into feature-rich product development. Phase two funding is conditional on phase one producing a published feasibility report, at least one formal institutional engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, or a related public-sector stakeholder, and a documented financing plan covering the remainder of the project.

Phase three (months 17–24) focuses on procurement, standards, and continuity intervention around AltID and related digital identity planning. Using the feasibility report, demonstrators, and coalition built in earlier phases, the project seeks inclusion of requirements stating that Danish digital identity systems should not depend exclusively on Apple or Google app stores, platform integrity APIs, or proprietary push-notification infrastructure, and should include a platform-neutral or otherwise certified fallback access path for critical public authentication. The project also engages with relevant EU bodies and technical working groups connected to the European Digital Identity Wallet framework, with the aim of aligning Danish advocacy with broader European requirements on interoperability, portability, resilience, and reduced platform lock-in. The project's role is not to dictate architecture directly, but to create technical evidence, procurement language, and standards pressure that make supplier-neutral and fallback-capable design harder to exclude. If formal traction with AltID is weak by month 16, phase three should de-scope toward publication, coalition consolidation, and EU-facing standards input rather than pretending Danish procurement influence has been secured.

The project team should include a lead researcher in mobile security and authentication protocols, a regulatory and compliance specialist familiar with Danish and EU digital identity frameworks (including eIDAS and NSIS), a policy and public-affairs coordinator experienced in Danish digital governance and procurement processes, a technical lead for the demonstrator work, and at least one additional engineer or contractor covering web authentication, hardware-token workflows, or Linux/GrapheneOS-related implementation. The technical staffing should avoid dependence on a single specialist. Assume the project's primary physical base is in Copenhagen, Denmark, at a Danish university, independent research institution, or security-qualified R&D facility providing access-controlled workspace appropriate for security-sensitive digital identity research, development, and stakeholder meetings. Budget for institutional overhead, external security review, and limited legal/procurement support explicitly rather than treating them as absorbed costs.

Success criteria: by month 24, the project has produced a published feasibility and risk report on platform-neutral and fallback-capable Danish digital identity; delivered two working non-production demonstrators (one mobile-oriented, one browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback); secured a formal written response from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or another relevant authority to the project's proposal; and achieved inclusion of platform-neutrality, fallback access, continuity, resilience, or supplier-concentration language in at least one official AltID-related design, policy, consultation, or procurement document. A stretch goal is that the project's EU-level engagement contributes to language in relevant European Digital Identity Wallet materials that supports platform-neutral access or certified fallback mechanisms. Do not use consumer adoption rates as a primary KPI for this project, because it is not shipping a production identity product.

Pick a realistic scenario that accounts for institutional inertia, regulatory friction, incumbent resistance, financing uncertainty, and the likelihood that convenience arguments will be used against platform-neutral alternatives. Do not assume constructive cooperation from existing operators. The primary lever is not technical disruption for its own sake, but the combination of resilience framing, procurement intervention, standards pressure, and credible technical demonstration.
